title: occasion: Mrs Wilmot
short: Written in June 1814 after Byron saw his cousin by marriage, Anne Wilmot, at a party, dressed in mourning with spangles.
body: James Wedderburn Webster recalled taking Byron to Lady Sitwell's party on 11 June 1814, where he first saw 'the beautiful Mrs. Wilmot', in mourning with spangles on her dress; Byron drank a tumbler of brandy to her health and wrote the poem the next day. E. H. Coleridge identifies her as Anne Beatrix Horton, wife of Byron's second cousin Robert John Wilmot. The black dress with points of light may underlie the poem's opening simile of a starry night. 'Walks in beauty' suggests that beauty is an atmosphere she moves through, not only a quality she has.

sources.cite: The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. III, ed. E. H. Coleridge (London: Murray, 1900), Introduction to Hebrew Melodies and note to 'She Walks in Beauty'

title: Hebrew Melodies
short: The poem opens Byron's Hebrew Melodies (1815), lyrics written to be set to traditional Jewish tunes by Isaac Nathan.
body: Through Douglas Kinnaird, Byron met the young composer Isaac Nathan and gave him lyrics to set to synagogue melodies; Nathan's folio, with music by Nathan and John Braham, appeared in April 1815, and Murray published the poems separately. Most are biblical, but E. H. Coleridge notes that 'She walks in Beauty' is one of three love poems in a collection whose title is 'somewhat misleading'. Nathan recalled that Byron often asked for this song. The poem was written before the project but placed first.

sources.cite: The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. III, ed. E. H. Coleridge (London: Murray, 1900), Introduction to Hebrew Melodies and note to 'She Walks in Beauty'

title: like the night
short: The surprising simile: beauty compared not to day or the sun but to a clear starry night.
body: Conventional love poetry compares the beloved to the sun, dawn or the rose. Byron chooses night, which allows the poem to mix dark and bright. The enjambment ('like the night / Of cloudless climes') delays the qualification: it is not any night, but a southern, cloudless one full of stars. The simile matches the occasion of a lady in black spangled mourning.

sources.cite: The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. III, ed. E. H. Coleridge (London: Murray, 1900), Introduction to Hebrew Melodies and note to 'She Walks in Beauty'

title: climes
short: Regions, countries (with their climate); "cloudless climes" suggests the clear night skies of the south.
body: 'Clime' was a poetic word for region or zone (from Greek klima, a zone of latitude). Byron, who had travelled in Greece and the Levant (1809-11), uses it often in his Eastern poems. The alliteration of 'cloudless climes' and 'starry skies' gives the second line its balanced music. The geographical word quietly brings into a London drawing-room the exotic settings of Byron's verse tales.

title: dark and bright
short: The poem's governing idea: perfect beauty is a balance of opposites, darkness and light meeting in harmony.
body: The line announces the structure of the whole lyric: the contrast of dark and light (night/stars, raven hair/lightened face) and their reconciliation. 'Aspect' means her look or appearance, both face and bearing. The balance is aesthetic and moral: the final stanza claims that this outward harmony expresses inward goodness. Some critics see a neoclassical ideal of balance in a poet usually associated with Romantic extremes.

sources.cite: The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. III, ed. E. H. Coleridge (London: Murray, 1900), Introduction to Hebrew Melodies and note to 'She Walks in Beauty'

title: gaudy day
short: Daylight is "gaudy", showy and garish, compared with the softer light of her beauty; there is an echo of Shakespeare's "gaudy, blabbing" day.
body: 'Gaudy' means showy, tastelessly bright. In 2 Henry VI 4.1 the scene opens with 'The gaudy, blabbing, and remorseful day / Is crept into the bosom of the sea'. Byron's 'tender light' is the light of evening or night that heaven 'denies' to day: day is too bright to have it. The phrase reverses the usual preference for daylight. The contrast is of tone rather than of value.

title: One shade the more ...
short: The balance is so exact that one more shadow or one less ray of light would have spoiled it.
body: The line is a perfect example of Byron's antithetical style, with the two halves mirroring each other. It suggests beauty as precise proportion, a classical idea. 'Had half impaired' means 'would have half spoiled': the conditional is in older syntax (pluperfect subjunctive). The idea of beauty as a perfect mean, where any addition or subtraction would spoil the whole, goes back to classical aesthetics, and the line performs that balance in its own symmetry.

sources.cite: The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. III, ed. E. H. Coleridge (London: Murray, 1900), Introduction to Hebrew Melodies and note to 'She Walks in Beauty'

title: nameless grace
short: An indefinable charm, the "je ne sais quoi"; Pope speaks of "nameless graces which no methods teach".
body: The idea of a grace beyond rules or description goes back to classical rhetoric and was a commonplace of eighteenth-century criticism. Pope's Essay on Criticism (1711) says that in music and poetry there are 'nameless graces which no methods teach, / And which a master hand alone can reach'. Byron admired Pope greatly. The grace 'waves' in her hair and 'lightens' over her face: it is a movement, not a fixed feature.

sources.cite: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part I ('nameless graces which no methods teach')

title: raven tress
short: Black hair (raven-coloured); a "tress" is a lock or plait of hair.
body: The black of the hair supplies the 'dark' element of the balance, and the lightening of the face the 'bright'. 'Tress' is a poetic word for a lock of hair. 'Raven' as an adjective of colour is conventional in romance. The verbs 'waves' and 'lightens' give the grace motion, so that her beauty is not a still portrait but something alive; Byron preferred dark beauties throughout his verse.

title: dwelling-place
short: Her face is the home where her thoughts live, and it expresses how pure and dear that home is.
body: The second stanza shifts from looks to mind. The syntax is compressed: her thoughts, 'serenely sweet', express how pure and dear their dwelling-place (her mind, or her face as the house of the mind) is. The image of the body as the mind's house is old and biblical (2 Corinthians 5:1, 'our earthly house of this tabernacle'). The poem thus moves outward to inward across its three stanzas.

anchor: So soft, so calm, yet eloquent
title: eloquent
short: Expressive: her face speaks without words.
body: The beauty is quiet, but it communicates. The third stanza is built on triple repetitions ('So soft, so calm', 'The smiles that win, the tints that glow'), and the face 'tells' of her life. 'Tints' are colours of the complexion, the 'bright' counterpart to the 'raven' hair. The word comes from Latin eloqui, 'to speak out': the quiet face 'speaks out' her character, so the poem's last lines can read virtue in her complexion and smile.

title: outward beauty, inward goodness
short: The final lines claim that her beauty expresses virtue: a life spent in goodness, a mind at peace, an innocent heart.
body: The poem ends not on physical beauty but on moral character, a Platonic idea (beauty as the outward sign of goodness) common in the Renaissance. 'All below' means everything on earth. The final exclamation, 'A heart whose love is innocent!', has struck some readers as ironic given Byron's reputation in 1814, others as sincere idealisation of a woman he barely knew. The form is three six-line stanzas in iambic tetrameter, rhymed ababab.

sources.cite: The Works of Lord Byron: Poetry, vol. III, ed. E. H. Coleridge (London: Murray, 1900), Introduction to Hebrew Melodies and note to 'She Walks in Beauty'
